title: Nepal seek redemption against Afghanistan 12 years after Incheon heartbreak - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal seek redemption against Afghanistan 12 years after Incheon heartbreak  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The 2014 Asian Games in Incheon, South Korea, remain a heart-breaking memory for Nepali cricket. Twelve years ago, the national team stood on the brink of history, presented with a glorious opportunity to secure the country’s first-ever medal in a team event on the continental stage.

After advancing from the group stage, Nepal faced Afghanistan in the quarterfinals. A victory would have set up a semifinal clash against Hong Kong—an opponent well within Nepal’s reach—with the then head coach Pubudu Dassanayake confidently targeting a place in the final.

Nepal executed their plan brilliantly in the first half, restricting Afghanistan—the team Nepal had defeated in the 2014 T20 World Cup in March—to a modest 119/9. But their batting faltered when it mattered most. Nepal managed only 111/7 in reply, falling agonisingly short by eight runs .

Now, Nepal have the chance for redemption as they take on Afghanistan at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Fast bowler Sompal Kami is the lone player from that 2014 squad. Making his return to the national side in Nagoya after missing the ACC Premier Cup, Kami is among a wave of players making their comeback, including Kushal Bhurtel, Kushal Malla, Aarif Sheikh and Nandan Yadav.

Except for Malla, the rest had been sidelined following a disappointing ICC CWC League-2 campaign in the Netherlands in July. In their absence, a revised Nepali side won the ACC Premier Cup in Malaysia to qualify for the 2027 Asia Cup, where they will feature alongside India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.

In Nagoya, Nepal are placed in a three-team group alongside Afghanistan and hosts Japan. A top-two finish in the group will propel Nepal into the quarterfinals, where Asian powerhouses India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh—all granted direct entry into the last eight—await.

Friday’s fixture will be Nepal’s opening match of the tournament. Afghanistan, meanwhile, kicked off their campaign on Thursday with an 81-run victory over Japan. Batting first, Afghanistan posted 129/6 before getting the hosts all out for 81 in 19.3 overs.

The pitch at Korogi Sports Park, which saw high-scoring games during the women’s competition, produced a run drought on the opening day of the men’s event on Thursday.

The Afghani side in Nagoya is not at full strength, lacking major stars including captain Rashid Khan. As a result, they struggled to show their typical aggressive batting. In another match at the venue, Hong Kong were restricted to 81/9 in 20 overs before Malaysia comfortably chased the target down in just 12 overs. Oman are the other team in the group of Hong Kong and Malaysia.

After cricket was omitted from the 2018 Jakarta-Palembang Games, Nepal made global headlines at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games by shattering a flurry of world records against Mongolia before being halted by India in the quarterfinals.

title: Nepal women lock up kabaddi bronze, target bigger prize - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal women lock up kabaddi bronze, target bigger prize  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Teams reaching the semifinals in kabaddi at the 20 th Asian Games secure at least a bronze medal. On Thursday, the Nepali women’s team did just that, defeating Sri Lanka 34-25 in the group stage. Nepal led in both halves—19-13 and 15-12—to register a comfortable win.

Sri Lanka fought back bravely in the second half, leaning on disciplined defence and well-timed Super Tackles to stem the tide. Yet, every time the pressure mounted, Nepal responded with composure—snatching vital bonus points on the mat and matching Sri Lanka with counter-striking Super Tackles to keep the lead firmly in their hands.

Nepal’s captain Manmati Bist executed a calm and decisive final raid in the dying seconds of the match, crossing back safely with milliseconds remaining to wrap up the victory before the final whistle blew on Sri Lanka’s last attempt.

The final whistle triggered jubilant scenes on the mat at Tokai Citizen Gymnasium, where the Nepali team celebrated a hard-fought semifinal berth that locked up at least a bronze medal.

Nepal women’s kabaddi team, a bronze medallist of the 19 th Asian Games, has made sure they will return with a bronze again, but they are hungry for more.

“We are very happy for back-to-back medals in the Asian Games,” Bist told journalists after the win against Sri Lanka. “Every player and staff member has been working very hard for this.”

Bist also praised the government, the National Sports Council and the All Nepal Kabaddi Association for their continuous support to the team.

“We got to train properly for about two years, competing at different international tournaments,” Bist added. “It was because of the international exposure and training we got that we could bounce back against Thailand and reach the semifinals today by defeating Sri Lanka.”

Nepal were trailing 15-24 in the first half against Thailand, before making a comeback in the second half to win the match 46-43. However, they had suffered a heavy defeat at the hands of Chinese Taipei on Wednesday, losing 37-18.

Still, the team seemed confident, unfazed by the loss against Chinese Taipei, when they entered the gymnasium for the decisive match against Sri Lanka.

“We had faced Sri Lanka many times over the years. We knew their players well,” said Parbati Rai, head coach of the women’s team. “I am not underestimating Sri Lanka, but we were confident of winning.”

Rai was also the head coach of the team when Nepal won bronze in the previous edition of the Asian main event in Hangzhou, China. “And to win a medal back-to-back, this means a lot to me as I am at the end of my coaching career,” she added.

Meanwhile, Rai and Bist argued that the win over Sri Lanka and securing a bronze did not end their hunger.

Placed in Group B, Nepal defeated Thailand in the first group-stage fixture on Tuesday while losing to Chinese Taipei (18-37) on Wednesday. They entered the semifinals as the second-placed team of Group B.

According to the tournament format, the top two teams from two groups progress to the semifinals, with the group topper facing the runner-up of the other group. Nepal, as the group runner-up, will face India, Group A’s topper. Similarly, Chinese Taipei, topper of Group B, will face Iran, second-placed team of Group A.

“We still have a match remaining,” Rai said. “And why would we not want to get a bigger medal this time?”

There are six players—Bist, Menuka Kumari Rajbanshi, Jayanti Badu, Rabina Chaudhary, Sirjana Kumari Tharu and Ganga Ghimire—in the current squad who helped Nepal clinch bronze in China.

Despite India, the undisputed world champions of kabaddi, being the opponent in the semis, the Nepali squad is unfazed.

“We know India is a tough opponent,” Bist said. “But we are also not a weak team. The new players have also got sufficient international exposure and training. Winning and losing is a different thing, but we are happy that we are not returning empty-handed.”

The semifinals will take place at Tokai Citizen Gymnasium on Friday, and the final will be held on Saturday. If Nepal win their semifinal match, they will secure silver and compete for the gold. But if they lose, they will have to settle for the bronze.

full_article:
KATHMANDU: Nepal and Namibia have established diplomatic relations, taking the number of countries with which Nepal maintains diplomatic ties to 187.

Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, who is in New York to attend the 81st United Nations General Assembly, and Namibia’s Minister of International Relations and Trade Selma Ashipala Musavyi signed a joint statement formalizing the establishment of diplomatic relations.

Before the signing ceremony, the foreign ministers of the two countries held discussions on various matters of mutual interest, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The ministers also discussed the loss of life and damage to infrastructure caused by the recent catastrophic climate disaster in Nepal. They emphasized the need to strengthen cooperation for the common progress and prosperity of the two countries and their peoples and explored new areas for expanding bilateral cooperation between Nepal and Namibia.

The disaster also affected areas in Tibet.

Floods in Nepal were triggered by a massive collapse in the high Himalayas along the Nepal-China border. A huge mass of rock and glacier ice broke away from Langtang Lirung late last month and plunged thousands of feet into a river, unleashing a powerful flood that swept downstream at devastating speed.

More than 5,000 people remained unaccounted for in Nepal in the days following the disaster, according to official figures, while hundreds more were reported missing on the Chinese side. Reuters reported that at least 1,386 people had died and more than 5,130 remained unaccounted for in Nepal as of September 18.

Balendra Shah said the catastrophe showed how climate-related risks in the Himalayas can quickly cross political boundaries.

“Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports," he said, making the case for regional systems that can share information and provide warnings before disasters strike.

‘Nepal Contributes Less Than 0.1% Of Global Emissions’

Balendra Shah said Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions but is paying what he described as a “colossal price" for the climate crisis.

“Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development," he said, adding, “For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency."

The Nepali PM said climate disasters were damaging roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and livelihoods, while also hitting the country’s clean-energy infrastructure. He said the destruction was forcing a developing country to borrow money to repair infrastructure damaged by a crisis it did not cause.

The recent floods caused extensive damage to hydropower projects and other infrastructure, adding to the economic burden as Nepal begins the long process of reconstruction. Nepal has estimated the reconstruction bill from the disaster at billions of dollars.

Balendra Shah used his UN address to propose a “Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism" led by Nepal, India and China. Under the proposed mechanism, the three countries would share satellite data and technical expertise, monitor dangerous glacial lakes and strengthen joint early-warning systems.

“When disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance across borders," Balendra Shah said. He argued that the Himalayas should become a centre of international cooperation rather than a region where critical information remains fragmented.

title: Nepal PM says floods ‘a warning to the world’ about climate change - The Straits Times
description: Nepal PM says floods ‘a warning to the world’ about climate change  The Straits Times
publisher.title: The Straits Times
full_article:
NEW YORK – Nepal’s catastrophic flooding in Aug ust “was a warning to the world” about the rising dangers of climate change, Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations on Sept 24, urging countries to step up to help his country adapt.

Addressing the General Assembly in sunglasses during its high-level week, Shah said a warming climate was “destabili s ing the fragile Himalayan ecology”, melting permafrost and glaciers and accelerating hazards.

The nation suffered one of the worst catastrophes in its history late Aug ust when a tsunami-like flood, triggered by a high-altitude glacial mountain collapse along the Nepal-China border, cut a swathe of destruction.

More than 1,400 people died, 6,000 are still missing, and the economic devastation runs in the billions of dollars.

Scientists from the World Weather Attribution have described the event as a “compound crisis” in which local geological instability combined with long-term warming has led to glacier retreat and permafrost thaw.

“Nepal contributes less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emission. We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it,” he said.

Shah urged the international community to help bear the cost of helping his country adapt to climate change, because “Nepal cannot build resilience alone against a crisis made worse by the failure of global governance”.

He proposed to create what he called a “Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism”, which would include Nepal and its neighbo u rs India and China, and allow them to share satellite data and expertise, monitor glacial lakes and strengthen joint early warning systems.

A 36-year-old ex-rapper, Shah swept to power six months ago on a wave of youth-led anti-corruption protests, buoyed by optimism for change.

But the disaster has pushed climate diplomacy to the centr e of his premiership, overshadowing the anti-corruption agenda.

Nepal has asked the UN’s Loss and Damage fund for US$20 million (S$25.5 million) in aid, the maximum allowed, but a tiny fraction of what it needs – a preliminary assessment by the government has placed the cost of the disaster at US$5 billion.

The fund, established in 2022 in the aftermath of catastrophic floods in Pakistan, has yet to make even its first disbursement, and observers see Nepal as a key test of its credibility.

Earlier this week, the United States pledged an additional US$31 million in new flood recovery support.

Nepal’s foreign minister Shisir Khanal told AFP that the G - 7 informally promised support at a meeting on Sept 23, and Britain has also vowed to help. AFP

title: Nepal's leader, at UN, says recent floods serve as a 'warning to the world' about climate change - bozemandailychronicle.com

publisher.title: bozemandailychronicle.com
full_article:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Nepal's prime minister scolded fellow world leaders Thursday, saying the nation's recent deadly flood reminds a warming world that climate change keeps hurting people who didn't cause the crisis but now need help.

The August disaster “was not just a local tragedy. It was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: Have you really heard that warning?” Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday night. “Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest, the secretary-general of the United Nations warned about humanity about the madness and impending climate disaster.”

“That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard enough,” Shah said. “We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence. But we, the political leaders, have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require.”





International scientists have connected melting permafrost from climate — caused by burning coal, oil and gas — to the instability of the glacier, which partly collapsed and triggered a massive flood that has killed at least 1,400 people with even more still missing.

Shah said that Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1% of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding.

“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” said Shah, 36, a former rapper and engineer who is the youngest head of government to address the General Assembly this year. “Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.”

He said climate change ‘does not recognize borders’

In a black Dhaka topi, a traditional brimless Nepali hat, Shah spoke while wearing his signature dark sunglasses, which he uses for medical reasons. He said “the tragic consequences of a warming climate” tells the world that “climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports.”

Subeksha Khadka, a humanitarian and former Miss Nepal International, in an online interview, praised Shah's speech and echoed the warning: "This time Nepal has been on the target, but it could be anyone. This is our story right now, and it can be anybody else’s tomorrow. So it’s time to act.”

Shah didn't ask for a specific amount in aid, but he called the international financial aid system inadequate and too bureaucratic. This included a loss and damage fund agreed upon a few years ago for poor nations hit by climate disasters not of their own making.

“Climate finance must not become another bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years” maneuvering through when they need help. “When the house is burning, we do not ask a family to complete 50 forms. We act. This is what climate justice means.”

He exhorted the General Assembly to act on relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction — which are traditional international help concepts — but also “responsibility, reparation, resilience.” Reparation is a word and an issue that rankles industrial western nations like the United States, which is historically the world's biggest carbon emitter.

He says it's ‘not an isolated disaster’

Over the past 75 years, the United States has spewed about 1,500 times more carbon into the air than Nepal has, according to the Global Carbon Project, a group of scientists that track greenhouse gas emissions by countries. Historical emissions matter because carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for more than a century trapping heat.

The U.S. this week announced $31 million in aid to Nepal for flood recovery, which bring America's total financial help up to $36 million. It's less than 1% of what they need.

“Preliminary assessments indicate that from recent disaster alone, Nepal has suffered loss of over $5 billion, nearly 15% of our GDP and a third of our annual budget," Shisir Khanal, Nepal's foreign minister, said Wednesday at the UN climate summit. "Thus for Nepal, this catastrophe is not merely a humanitarian emergency. It is a development emergency dismantling years of progress. It is a justice crisis exposing the inequities of global climate action and it is an existential crisis striking at the very survival of our communities and our future.”

“What happened in Nepal is not an isolated disaster but a preview of what awaits many vulnerable nations,” Khanal said.

Former United States Vice President Al Gore said in an interview that Nepal's disaster shows that the climate crisis “was getting worse much faster” than people can handle and foreshadows problems with melting glaciers that feed all of the great rivers of Asia, putting the water supply of 2 billion people at risk.

Delgado reported from New York. Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report.

Former United States Vice President Al Gore said in an interview that Nepal's disaster shows that the climate crisis “was getting worse much faster” than people can handle and foreshadows problems with melting glaciers that feed all of the great rivers of Asia, putting the water supply of 2 billion people at risk.

___

Delgado reported from New York. Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report.

title: Balendra Shah UN speech: Full transcript of Nepal prime minister’s address to the 81st UN General Assembly - The Kathmandu Post
description: Balendra Shah UN speech: Full transcript of Nepal prime minister’s address to the 81st UN General Assembly  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and gentlemen,

I come before you from Nepal - a distant country in the Himalayas- carrying a close warning for humanity.

I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development,democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation.

Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epicproportions.

About families waiting for loved ones who will never come home.

About communities searching through mud, rocks and water forpeople whose bodies may never be recovered.

About bridges, roads, schools, homes and livelihoods swept away inminutes.

And about a country whose steady progress to achieve SustainableDevelopment Goals has been interrupted.

====

Four weeks ago, the world saw the shocking images of thecatastrophic flash floods that swept through Nepal’s mountain communities withferocity many have called a “Himalayan Tsunami.”

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy,it was a warning to the world.

And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?

Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our MountEverest, the Secretary-General of the United Nations warned humanity about themadness of an impending climate disaster.

That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard loudlyenough.

We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it.

Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it withevidence.

But we, the political leaders of the world, have been negligent totranslate those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable peoplerequire.

Last month, we saw the tragic consequences.

=====

A warming climate is destabilizing the fragile Himalayan ecology.

Melting permafrost are fracturing mountain slopes beneath theglaciers and accelerating the risks of ice-rock avalanche, floods, landslidesand other cascading hazards.

The resulting devastation unleashed havoc on both sides of theNepal-China border. The flood continued downstream towards India.

This tells us something fundamental:

Climate change does not recognize borders.

Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped onpassports.

Excellencies,

I am not here to complain but to share some suggestions.

First, I wish to express Nepal's deep gratitude to all those whocame to our aid in the aftermath of the deluge.

Our immediate neighbors, India and China, offered prompt andgenerous assistance.

Other friendly countries, the United Nations system, humanitarianagencies, philanthropies and people around the world stood with Nepal.

To all of them, I say: thank you on behalf of the gratefulpeople of Nepal.

Nepal now faces a massive task of recovery and reconstruction.

After at least 1400 confirmed deaths and over 6,000 people stillmissing, our rapid assessments peg physical recovery needs at about 10 percentof GDP.

As in rebuilding after past disasters like the 2015 Gorkhaearthquake, we count on your solidarity and support.

But we must also understand why this disaster matters beyondNepal.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of globalgreenhouse-gas emissions.

We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal pricefor it.

Our glaciers are retreating. Our mountain slopes are becomingunstable. Our rivers are becoming less predictable.

And every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.

For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event,but a development emergency.

It destroys roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and livelihoods.

It destroys clean energy infrastructure that we need to fuel ourfuture.

And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage itdid not cause.

=====

But we are not here to blame any country or continent.

We are not here to turn climate change into another geopoliticalbattlefield.

We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibilityand solidarity.

Through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change,the international community has already agreed to the principle of commonbut differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

Those who have historically contributed more to the problem, andthose with greater capacity to respond, must do more.

Climate Justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a UnitedNations Document.

People of our country be allowed to build their future instead ofconstantly rebuilding their past.

========

Excellencies,

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to nearly two billion people.These mountains provide water, ecosystems, agriculture and livelihoods topopulations far beyond Nepal.

The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part ofthe planet's life-support system.

That is why, as an urgent first step, we propose that weestablish a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India andChina.

Through this mechanism, let us share satellite data and expertise.

Let us monitor dangerous glacial lakes.

Let us strengthen joint early-warning systems.

And when disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance acrossborders.

Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of internationalcooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information.

Remarkable for a least developed country, Nepal is already playinga global role exceeding its ecological share.

We have restored forests to cover nearly half our territory.

We are installing hydro power at a pace enough to power all ourclean energy needs and displace dirty sources abroad.

We are promoting electric mobility with an adoption rate to matchparts of Europe.

We are strengthening climate adaptation at the local level. And weshall do more to withstand increased intensity and frequency of climatedisasters.

=====

But, Nepal cannot build resilience alone against a crisis madeworse by the failure of global governance.

That is why this Assembly must note six words:

Relief. Rehabilitation. Reconstruction.

And also:

Responsibility. Reparation. Resilience.

The first three are what we need after disaster.

The second three are what we need to ensure that disaster does notbecome a permanent condition.

When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of apoor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork ofsmall grants.

We need adequate grant-based support from the world. TheLoss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevantfinancing mechanisms remain grossly inadequate.

Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through whichvulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help.

When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to completefifty forms.

We act.

That is what climate justice must mean.

========

Excellencies,

This brings me to a larger question:

What kind of international order do we want?

The United Nations was born from humanity's experience of horrificWorld Wars.

Its promise was that sovereignty would matter.

International law would matter.

The dignity of every human being would matter.

And the weak would not simply have to accept whatever the powerfuldecide.

Today, that international system is under strain.

Too often, military and economic power determines whose voice isheard.

Nepal believes we need a much fairer global economic order.

========

In 1994, UNDP’s Human Development Report conceptualized the notionof human insecurity.

It equated security with people rather than territories, and withdevelopment rather than arms. It called for the peace dividend to secure freedomsfrom fear and want.

The new majoritygovernment in Nepal, elected through the fairest and most peaceful electionsin our history this March, has had to weather many international adversitiessince.

When a poorfarmer in Nepal went to sow her seeds this monsoon, fertilizers didn’t reachher on time. When we wanted to pave a new highway, there was no bitumen. When afamily sat down for an evening meal, there was shortage of cooking fuel.

On the one hand,there are melting glaciers and failing harvests to floods arriving withoutwarning. On the other, a global supply chain punishes poor people for causesbeyond reason.

Inter-continentalmissiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear everybottleneck, meet each deadline. But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure hisfertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.

We have built aworld with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food.

And this is not Nepal's privatemisfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. AskPakistan. Ask Sri Lanka. Ask any othercountry in our region and you will hear the same account: hit by the climatewe did not warm, and hit again by the wars we did not start.

This tells usthere is a lot more broken than meets the eye in the present order of globalcooperation.

Excellencies,

I am told I am the youngest Head ofGovernment to address this Assembly this year.

I did not come here to make that the story.

I came to make sure that whatever elseis said from this podium, one thing is said plainly: a country that iswilling to pay should be able to buy, and a world that can deliver a weaponanywhere in seventy-two hours has no excuse for leaving a farmer without meansfor a decent livelihood.

This is why we continue to believe in multilateralism. This is whywe need a United Nations in which the presence of small poor countries is felt,and we can work together towards just outcomes.

Climate justice is, therefore, not only about money.

It is about distributive justice - who bears the costs.

It is about procedural justice - who has a voice.

It is about whether the future of mountain communities, smallisland states, landlocked and least-developed countries, and generations yetunborn count equally.

Starting tomorrow at the “Sagarmatha to the Sea” side-event righthere at the United Nations, Nepal is ready to help lead this conversation.

======

Mr. President & Excellencies,

We are at this GeneralAssembly at a moment of profound global uncertainty — and with a reneweddemocratic mandate that reflects the aspirations of a new generation.

Our youth have demandeda politics of integrity and accountability.

This generational shiftis not only a national story. It is part of a global awakening againstconflicts, inequities, and lack of opportunities.

The commitment of mygovernment is clear: to build a state that delivers — decent jobs, socialprotection, and a fair chance for every Nepali to thrive at home.

The Nepal floods signala future shaped by rising climate extremes. Our baselines are no longerrelevant. And we must move from ad-hoc responses to a culture ofpreparedness.

Let us finance resilience, and invest in insurance and innovation.

Let us build stronger infrastructure and institutions.

Let us reduce fossil-fuel dependence.

Let us build systems that warn, alert and save lives.

Let us reform the order that leaves the weakest with the leastpower.

And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world:

Let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.

भगवान पशुपतिनाथले विश्वको कल्याण गरुन्।

यो विश्व बुद्धले देखाएको बाटोमा हिंड्न सकोस्।

title: In New York, Foreign Minister Khanal introduces Nepal’s new political order - The Kathmandu Post
description: In New York, Foreign Minister Khanal introduces Nepal’s new political order  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Less than a year after a Gen Z-led movement toppled Nepal’s government and six months after an election dramatically reordered the country’s politics, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal took to a stage in New York on Thursday to explain Nepal’s new political order to an international audience.

Speaking at the Asia Society on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Khanal offered a wide-ranging account of the forces that brought Prime Minister Balendra “Balen” Shah and the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) to power — from frustration over corruption and political instability to slow economic growth and the continued exodus of young Nepalis abroad.

For much of the hour-long Asia Society conversation, Kevin Rudd, the former Australian prime minister and the organisation’s president, played the role of an outsider trying to make sense of a political transformation that unfolded remarkably quickly.

“You’ve got three minutes to explain Nepali domestic politics to us,” Rudd said to Khanal. For “foreign barbarians like myself,” he joked, Nepal’s politics could be “more complex to understand than American politics.”

“Three minutes are probably not enough,” Khanal replied.

Khanal briefly walked the audience through Nepal’s political transitions before arriving at what he described as years of unstable governments, political patronage and “rampant corruption”. Those failures, he argued, produced a “deep distrust of political order”, particularly among young Nepalis.

But much of Khanal’s explanation focused on what was happening beyond politics. Nepal’s median age is around 26, he said, and young Nepalis have watched economies elsewhere in Asia expand while opportunities at home remained limited. At the same time, leaving the country has increasingly become part of young adulthood, with Nepalis travelling to the Gulf and East Asia for work and, increasingly, Eastern Europe.

“There’s been a huge outward flow of Nepali young people who have seen the world grow in front of their eyes, but have seen stagnation and rampant corruption at home,” Khanal said.

That frustration helped propel the Gen Z movement and, eventually, the RSP. The party, founded only in 2022, went from the fourth-largest force in Parliament to close to a two-thirds majority in the lower house following the March election, Khanal said.

When Rudd referred to Shah as “Nepal’s Mamdani”, Khanal agreed. But he argued that the outsider character of the new government extends beyond the prime minister.

“Pretty much all of us come from very non-political backgrounds in Nepali politics,” Khanal said. “We come from businesses, social sectors, and do not have a long history of being in politics.”

Khanal himself came from the education sector, having helped establish Teach for Nepal before later working as an education adviser to a local government. He entered Parliament with the RSP in 2022 and took on the fledgling party’s international affairs portfolio because, as he recalled Thursday, “nobody else was doing it.”

Now foreign minister, Khanal used his New York appearance to explain not only how the new political class arrived in government, but what it intends to do with power.

“Our focus is on strong social justice, but at the same time, pragmatism on economic policy,” he said. Khanal described the RSP as the first Nepali party to openly identify itself as economically liberal, favouring market liberalisation, reduced bureaucratic barriers and greater investment while pursuing progressive policies on education, healthcare and social security.

That economic agenda also sits at the centre of Khanal’s vision for Nepal’s foreign policy.

The government has set a goal of achieving middle-income status within a decade and high-income developed status by 2050, Khanal said. Foreign policy, in his telling, should help achieve that ambition by building productive industries, attracting investment and creating high-wage employment at home. Doing so, however, requires Nepal to think differently about its geography.

“Nepal is routinely described as a small country,” Khanal said. “But scale is purely relational.” Sitting between India and China makes Nepal appear small, he argued, but the size of its neighbours “must never become the ceiling of our ambition”.

“Nepal is not small,” he said. “Nepal is strategically positioned.”

Khanal described the government’s approach as “development autonomy”: using Nepal’s relationships with its neighbours and other partners abroad to expand the country’s economic options and create more opportunities at home. Instead of framing Nepal primarily as a small country caught between two larger powers, he argued that its location could itself become an economic advantage.

“Our question in this rising century is no longer how Nepal survives between two giants,” he said. “Our question is how does Nepal create value between them and beyond them?”

India is central to that calculation. Nepal shares more than 1,700 kilometres of open border with five Indian states—Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim—which together are home to more than 400 million people. Nearly two-thirds of Nepal’s trade is with India, Khanal said, while around 65 percent of its imports come from its southern neighbour.

Khanal described relations with New Delhi as “excellent”, while acknowledging their historical “ebb and flow”. He said the new government is trying to take a more pragmatic approach to Nepal’s neighbours, placing less emphasis on ideological differences and more on areas of economic cooperation. “Instead of focusing on where the challenges are, our approach right now is: where are the opportunities?” he said.

Hydropower is one. Nepal has around 43 gigawatts of economically viable hydropower potential, Khanal said, and the government hopes to expand electricity exports to India and Bangladesh. It also hopes that access to relatively inexpensive green energy and the vast market across the southern border can attract manufacturers to Nepal. Khanal described the strategy as one of “thick connectivity and thin borders”.

To the north, China offers another major market, but the Himalayas make physical connections considerably more difficult. China is Nepal’s second-largest trading partner, and Chinese investors are among the country’s largest foreign investors, Khanal said. His government hopes that better physical connections across the mountains can expand that economic relationship.

Nepal wants to improve roads across its northern frontier while pursuing tunnels, dry ports, aviation and digital links and, eventually, cross-border rail. But Khanal argued that the success of those projects should be measured by more than kilometres of infrastructure. What matters is whether they increase the movement of “goods, services, investment, tourists, and opportunity” and help transform Nepal “from a landlocked economy into a land-linked economy”.

Nepal signed a Belt and Road Initiative memorandum with China in 2017 and a framework agreement in December 2024, though Khanal said projects under the initiative have yet to enter implementation. His government, he added, would pursue cooperation with China based on “transparent financing, rigorous feasibility, and value for money principles” while preserving Nepal’s autonomy.

For Khanal, deeper ties with China need not come at the expense of Nepal’s relationship with India. “We do not see our northern and southern corridors as competing directions,” he noted repeatedly, stating that the country has the ability to turn its geography into a “gateway for commerce and opportunity”.

The United States fits differently into that vision. Khanal described Washington as a longstanding development partner, but said his government is particularly interested in attracting more US investment. He argued that significant economic potential between the two countries has yet to be fully realised, while also pointing to Europe, Japan, ASEAN countries and the Gulf as partners Nepal hopes to engage more deeply.

On security, however, Khanal was more cautious. When Rudd asked about the security dimension of the US relationship, Khanal was more cautious, pointinged to Nepal’s geography and foreign policy sensitivities. “Security alliance or security cooperation is something we do not strongly pursue,” he said, while noting that the two countries have historically cooperated in security-related areas.

Following the talk of Nepal’s relations with India, China and the United States, Khanal returned to what those relationships could actually deliver at home. “Foreign policy is always an extension of domestic policy,” he said.

Khanal said he hopes Nepal can become a more active economic corridor in South Asia, better connected to India and China while building relationships beyond its borders. But after an afternoon discussing trade, hydropower, investment,spent talking about trade, hydropower, investment and great-power politics, Khanal expressed hope for a future where Nepalis themselves saw a future in Nepal.

title: A month after Nepal-China floods, families await answers about more than 50 missing Ukrainians - WKMG
description: A month after Nepal-China floods, families await answers about more than 50 missing Ukrainians  WKMG
publisher.title: WKMG
full_article:
BANGKOK – Olena Kalynychenko was looking forward to sharing the chrysanthemum tea she had bought in China with her partner.

“She said, ‘When I come back home, we will drink the tea made from Chinese flowers,’” said Oles Visich, Kalynychenko’s partner. He has now been waiting for news about her for a month, after she and thousands of others disappeared in catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border.

Recommended Videos

Her last known location was exiting China at a border post at 10:22 a.m. local time, 15 minutes before the flood.

Kalynychenko, 36, was part of a group of 56 people, mostly Ukrainians, who had traveled to Mount Kailash in Tibet for a spiritual retreat.

Their families' situation is a sign of how complex and time-consuming the process is of rescuing, recovering and identifying victims lost to the disaster. Given the number of missing, the process will likely take months.

They disappeared while heading from China to Nepal on their way home. Some relatives say they have received no information from authorities. The Chinese government has told at least two families that their relatives left Chinese territory before the flood struck, but they haven't been able to confirm whether they entered Nepal as Nepal's immigration complex and its records were destroyed in the floods.

Little information is reaching families

The floods killed more than 1,400 people and left more than 6,000 missing, most of them on the Nepali side of the border. Nepal has said that 636 foreign nationals remain missing, including 54 Ukrainians. China has reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing on its side, including one Ukrainian.

Families in Ukraine say most of them have not received any answers since realizing their relatives were among the missing.

“We only have the statistics that are being posted online — how many people have been found, how many are alive, how many are dead, and how many are still missing,” said Stanislav Solohub, whose brother and sister-in-law went missing on Aug. 25.

Nepal says it has recovered 1,451 bodies, but only 112 have been handed over to families so far.

The government said it has collected DNA samples from 2,035 relatives so far, but it has not disclosed how many victims have been identified.

Last messages were sent minutes before the floods began

The group, led by Irina Blonskaya, a spiritual teacher who often organized retreats, was returning from its journey home in China when the flood struck Aug. 26. Their plan was to travel by bus from the Tibet region to Kathmandu, where its members would board flights to their respective countries. The group’s last message was sent at 8:27 a.m. Nepal time, about 10 minutes before the mountain slope collapsed.

Many had not checked in with their loved ones that morning, owing to the time difference.

Authorities have said the were triggered when a section of ice and rock broke away from a Himalayan mountain slope, creating a fast-moving torrent of water, ice, mud and debris. It destroyed communities and Gyirong Port, a border crossing used by some pilgrims traveling to or returning from Mount Kailash.

‘Who is looking for them?’

Vladsylava Horlova’s mother, Elena, was traveling in the group as well. She initially found her mother’s name of the list of the missing from the Nepali government, but hasn't received any further information from the Nepali side. Later, the Chinese embassy confirmed her mother had left the country, and was not counted in China's list of missing people.

Horlova, a college student who is a refugee in Norway, worries her mother wasn't in either country when the flood struck. There’s a stretch of road between the Nepali immigration building and the Chinese one along the border, videos from travelers show.

“You think about what if someone appeared to be in a no man’s land or that they left China, but not physically, who’s looking for them?” she asked.

Horlova has attempted to contact organizations ranging from the Ukrainian embassy in China, to Norwegian police, and even the Red Cross. She, like the others, have submitted their DNA samples to police to help the search.

On the other side of the border, China has said that when the remains of foreigners are identified, it will notify their respective embassies, but the authorities have not given any details about how many identities have been confirmed so far.

People still have hope

Though it has been a month since the original disaster, some families are still holding on to hope.

Just days before Kalynychenko left for her travels, she organized a retreat for women in Ukraine whose partners were fighting on the front lines of the war, some of whom had not heard from their partners for two years.

Visich, her partner, sees the irony of his situation, but like others in the group, has chosen to stay positive. Visich, also a psychologist, wrote a support guide for others like himself, offering tips on mental health.

“Because for my Olenka, for example, the most important thing in our connection, that each other … needs to be happy,” Visich said.

___

AP writer Binaj Gurubacharya in Kathmandu, Nepal and senior video producer Volodymr Yurchuk in Kyiv, Ukraine contributed to this report.
